questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I have family living in the U.S. and I wanted to be closer to them. Additionally, Vermont Law and Graduate School (VLGS) had an interesting environmental profile that offered some academic opportunities.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, I enjoyed my time in Vermont, as I got to experience living in a completely different environment than I am used to. Small town life is slow and sometimes I got bored, but it can be cute too, and it made me focus on my academics. I also got to experience other places in the US, like Boston (MA), Miami (FL), NYC (NY), and Portland (ME) - places I'd never been to. If I had planned better, I could've definitely planned more trips.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy thanks to the international admissions counselor at VLGS. She helped me with everything and even checked up on me on her own initiative. Since the school is small, the staff is always available to help out. If you're considering going on exchange at VLGS, I recommend contacting their admissions office, as they will be happy to help you with any questions, you might have.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I was picked up at Burlington Airport by a staff member and he drove me to my housing, which was very nice. When we arrived at my housing, he made sure that I had everything I needed, and even got me a shower curtain and some pots and pans.

You can either fly to Burlington which is closer, or Boston and then take the Dartmouth Coach to Lebanon. A staff member can pick you up in either Burlington or Lebanon.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
The school had an international orientation before the orientation week, which meant that I met the other international students before everyone else. Knowing some students already made it easier going into the orientation week.

The first week of the semester is fully dedicated to orientation, and all the new law and graduate students are there to meet each other. There are people from all over the country and no one knows each other. It was a nice and mostly informal week, where I met a lot of new people in a relaxed and non-academic setting.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I was lucky, as the international admissions counselor reached out to me about housing, so I didn't have to look very much. But I recommend starting the housing hunt in spring, as I've heard that it can be difficult to find housing since the town is small. 

Again, reach out to admissions to ask for their help, and sign up for the VLGS housing portal.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
There is no housing on campus, so the only option is to find something off campus. Make sure to find a place with a nice landlord. I lived alone but looking back, I wish i would've had a roommate as I enjoy spending time with others more than being alone. 

If you plan to live in South Royalton, find something close to campus, as walking will be cold in the winter.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
South Royalton itself is walkable, but if you find housing outside of South Royalton you will need a car.

Don't be scared if the housing doesn't have a washer/dryer, as the gym has those.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I wasn't allowed to sign up for JD classes, which is the classes that are mandatory for the law students. Looking back, I wish I would've fought to be allowed to take a JD class, as most of the friends I made at orientation were in those classes. The classes that the first year law students had were Legal Writing, Civil Procedure, Torts, and Contracts. 

When I applied for advanced approval from UCPH I had to e-mail the registrar's office, as the course listings from VLGS didn't have all the needed information.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I e-mailed the registrar's office and they assigned me to the courses that I wanted.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The registrar's helped me answer questions before and after my arrival. After my arrival, I booked a meeting with the Vice Dean for Faculty and she talked with me about the courses I had chosen.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was unsuccessful in registering for Constitutional Law, as it is a JD class, but othr than that i got all the courses I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look into the possibility of taking first year JD classes, as you will be able to spend much more time with your friends. Don't take the first no as an answer and maybe ask UCPH for a letter of approval of your legal ability.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Some classes were amazing, some were less amazing. It mostly depended on the professor.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses were more or less the same level as those in Denmark, of course with the added challenge of having a class in english. The courses was not a law-heavy as in Denmark.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Most of my classes were small with less that ten students. These classes were generally focused around a class discussion where all students were able to equally contribute and asks questions.

My larger classes were much like what I remember high school being like with rows of table and a professor going through the topic of the day. 

In all my classes, I was partially graded on my performance in class.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Energy Law & Policy in a Carbon Constrained World (ENG5226 01 E) 3 credits
- Negotiation (ADR6420) 2 credits
- Climate Change: Power of Taxes (CLM5365 01) 2 credits
- International Climate Change Law (ENV5218 01) 3 credits
- International & Comparative Environmental Law (INT7444 01) 2 credits

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Negotiation! The professors are great, and the course is fun and different, as it mostly consists of simulations of negotiations.

Climate Change: Power of Taxes was my absolute favorite course. Professor Milne is and expert in this field, and it was obvious that the course was well thought-out.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Housing costs above is excluding utilities which ranged from 400 DKK to 900 DKK depending on the month. Utilities can be expensive during winter month because of heating costs.

The local transportation covers the Dartmouth Coach which I took when traveling to Boston or NYC. My friends would never ask me for gas money when I drove with them.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Books. I was able to lend all the books from the on-campus library. Some of my courses didn't have any required books and instead all readings were available on Canva.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were some activities like the hockey team, basketball team, and outdoor club, but it was a bit sparse. There was a sporting event in the beginning of the semester and that was really fun, though.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of community dinners during the semester where you can come and eat with your friends often for free.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
In summer, enjoy the warm weather and take a swim in the river. Go hiking, and explore the beautiful nature. 
Go to Fable Farm Fermentory every Thursday and enjoy the food, wine, music, camp fires, and starlit sky - it is the nicest way to spend your Thursday evening. 

Go skiing, ice skating, snow tubing, and any other winter activity you might find.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Visit big cities like Boston, NYC, Montreal, or fly out to any place in the country from Boston Airport. 

Definitely go to Portland, Maine, on a day trip! Coziest city ever. I went in September and loved it. Try a Maine lobster roll.

Don't miss out on the Tunbridge Fair! So much fun and a true American experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, americans are welcoming, friendly, and easy to get to know.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Invite yourself if you hear of something you'd like to join! During orientation, this is how I met my friends, and since everyone is new, they won't mind you joining, they'll think it's nice to get to know you.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Though I enjoyed the friendliness of Americans, it did make it a bit harder figuring out who actually wanted to be friends, and who was just being overly nice. You'll figure it out, just give it time.

I expected the tipping culture to be different, but still had to adjust and ask my friends what was expected.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Vermont is a relatively progressive state, and I felt very safe there considering the current political climate. Generally, the Americans students that I befriended were nothing like the stereotypical American.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Consider getting or leasing a car. As a minimum, make sure that you have an international license - maybe a friend will let you borrow their car.
- Enjoy and explore the nature. 
- Use the professor's and TA's office hours.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I can't stress enough that you should reach out to VLGS with any questions you might have whether you have accepted a spot or not. They are very helpful and made my stay there so much easier.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The feeling of completing a semester on exchange and the independence it brought me. I also felt very accomplished academically, as attendance is mandatory, and I really got to focus on my courses.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
I was homesick, and sometimes felt lonely. Looking back, I wish I would've reached out more to my friends at the school and asked them to hang out, as I later found out that many of my friends were lonely too. 

The lack of public transportation was a challenge too, as I couldn't really go anywhere without a friend or a student ambassador to drive me. I wish I would've had a car to go explore by myself.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
This is not the classic exchange experience like in a big city where there is something new to do every day. The town is small, and you will be seeing the same people, but take it as an experience and just be sure to be proactive in planning activities. The people there are lovely and very open to getting to know you. 

The outdoors in Vermont are something special and definitely something you won't experience anywhere else. If you're not into the outdoors, then take as many trips to the surrounding big cities as possible. It's easy to get to Boston Airport.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
